title: Transmission Control Protocol
about: Authored against RFC 9293 §3.1 directly. Nothing here was converted from a document, so nothing here
is shaped by what a document could say.
Two things are worth reading before the nodes. First, TCP has exactly ONE header format — the RFC
calls §3.1 'Header Format', singular — so there is one message node. What varies between a SYN segment
and an established one is not the format but which options may appear in it, and that is what the two
packings are for. Second, every field is a node, including the four-bit and one-bit ones: a control bit
is a field that happens to be one bit wide, not a slice of a byte that some other node owns.
Sets follow the RFC's own headings. §3.1 describes a header, and inside it a group it names 'Control
bits'; both are sets here, and the second nests in the first. Sets hold; they do not produce. That is
why a length can measure a header while the header writes nothing of its own.
Where a walk begins. Its ways on are the message formats TCP declares — one, here — and they hang
off it by the same edge a packing hangs off a message and a field hangs off the one before it.
It is a node rather than a list beside the graph so that 'which message is this?' is asked in the
same place, and the same way, as every other choice in the description.

nodes.about: RFC 9293 §3.1. The only message format TCP has.

about: RFC 9293 §3.1, Maximum Segment Size option: 'This field may be sent in the initial connection
request (i.e., in segments with the SYN control bit set) and MUST NOT be sent in other segments.'
That is a decisive change in what the options span may contain, decided by state, which is what a
second packing is for. The header itself is identical in both.

nodes.about: The same header, with the Maximum Segment Size option not an option at all.
RFC 9293 §3.1. What Data Offset measures, and what the checksum covers after the pseudo-header.
RFC 9293 §3.1: 'The source port number.' 16 bits.
RFC 9293 §3.1: 'The destination port number.' 16 bits.

about: RFC 9293 §3.1: the sequence number of the first data octet in this segment, except that when SYN
is set it is the initial sequence number and the first data octet is ISN+1.
RFC 9293 §3.1: the next sequence number the sender expects. Significant only when ACK is set.
A DIFFERENT NODE from the ACK control bit, though a reader skimming would call both 'ack'. One is
a 32-bit number and the other is one bit saying whether that number means anything. Same syllable,
unrelated concepts, so they are not the same field.
RFC 9293 §3.1: 'The number of 32-bit words in the TCP header.' 4 bits.
Its own node, with its own width — not a slice of an octet belonging to something else.

RFC 9293 §3.1: the number of data octets the sender of this segment is willing to accept.

about: RFC 9293 §3.1: 'the 16-bit ones' complement of the ones' complement sum of all 16-bit words in the
header and text', computed over a pseudo-header prefixed to the segment.
The pseudo-header is a set here (see pseudoHeader) rather than something the checksum converter
knows about privately. It is laid out and then read as input, which keeps the fact that TCP's
checksum reaches outside its own header a visible part of the description.

nodes.about: RFC 9293 §3.1: 'only to be interpreted in segments with the URG control bit set.'

about: RFC 9293 §3.1: 'Options may occupy space at the end of the TCP header and are a multiple of 8 bits
in length.' The span runs from the end of the fixed 20 octets to wherever Data Offset says the
header ends, so it is empty whenever Data Offset is 5.
RFC 9293 §3.1. ONE node, shared by every option, and this is the sharing rule doing real work: the
leading octet of an End-of-Option-List, a No-Operation and a Maximum Segment Size is the same
concept — which option this is — so it is one field, not three that happen to look alike.
What differs between options is the value it takes on a given appearance, and a value belongs to
the run, not to the description.
Where the option list forks on what optionKind said. A junction rather than a set: it makes no
octets and holds nothing — the kind octet is already written and each arm carries its own rest.
RFC 9293 §3.1, Kind 0. A single octet, already written as optionKind, so this arm adds nothing —
which is exactly a junction rather than an empty set.

nodes.about: RFC 9293 §3.1, Kind 1. One octet, used to align a following option on a word boundary.

about: Where the arms meet. A junction because it makes no octets and holds nothing — it exists so the
arms have one place to converge on, and so skipping the whole options set has somewhere to skip
TO: the walk leaves an absent set from where its last member would have led.

nodes.about: RFC 9293 §3.1, Kind 2, Length 4. Reachable only from the synchronising packing.

about: RFC 9293 §3.1: 'The option-length counts the two octets of option-kind and option-length as well as
the option-data octets.' Shared for the same reason optionKind is.

nodes.about: The option's data: the largest segment the sender of this SYN is willing to receive.
Everything after the header. Its extent is what the carrier says, less the header.

about: RFC 9293 §3.1: 96 bits prefixed to the segment for the checksum, and never transmitted. A set with
no step on the message path reaching it — it is laid out because the checksum requires it, which
is the only reason anything here is ever laid out.

nodes.label: Length 4
nodes.about: RFC 9293 §3.1: the MSS option is four octets — kind, length, and two of data.

nodes.label: header words
about: RFC 9293 §3.1: Data Offset is the number of 32-bit words in the header. Measured off the header
set rather than declared, which is why the header is a set: it is the thing with an extent.

nodes.label: TCP length
nodes.about: RFC 9293 §3.1: header plus data, not counting the pseudo-header.

nodes.label: is SYN set?
about: What picks the packing. A value that keys the ways on, rather than a condition on each — sibling
conditions cannot be proved to cover, and a segment matching neither would bind nothing and say
nothing about it.

nodes.label: which option is this?
nodes.about: What keys the option fork. Read on the way in, written from the selected arm on the way out.

nodes.label: the datagram's source address
about: An outside value is not a computation — it is something a computation may require. So a field fed
from outside is fed by an evaluation that reads it, and the edge to the outside node says where it
came from. One node more than it looks like it needs, and the thing that produces the value is
always the same kind of thing.

nodes.label: are there options?
about: What decides the optional step into the options span. An optional step with nothing deciding it
is a definition error rather than a permitted default — there is no honest thing to do with one,
since guessing from leftover octets makes presence depend on what came after.

nodes.label: is there data?
about: A segment with no data is ordinary — a bare ACK is exactly that — so this is a real question and
not a degenerate case. On the way in the carrier's extent answers it; on the way out, whether a
payload was supplied.

nodes.label: ones' complement sum
about: RFC 9293 §3.1. A converter — arithmetic over octets — not a TCP-specific step: what makes it TCP's
checksum is the three things required into it, which are named on the edges and not in here.

nodes.because: RFC 9293 §3.1: Rsrvd must be zero in a generated segment.
A header is at least five 32-bit words and Data Offset is four bits, so 5..15.

about: TCP has one message format, so this is the unbranched case: one way on, no key, nothing to decide.
A protocol with a request and a response would have two of these, keyed and decided exactly as the
two packings below are — same edge, same mechanism, one scale up.

edges.about: Which arrangement this segment takes is decided by the SYN bit.

about: A set is a place on the path, not a bracket around one. The walk arrives at the header and goes on
to its first member; leaving the last member leaves the header. That is what lets an absent set be
one step over all of its members at once.
The options span is empty when Data Offset is 5, so the step into it may not be taken. The step is
into the SET, which is what makes 'no options' one skipped step rather than a separate arrangement.
What may turn up in the options span, and how many turn up is a fact about a segment rather than
about TCP — so there is no count anywhere in this description and no way on that reaches back.

edges.because: RFC 9293 §3.1: Rsrvd must be zero in generated segments.
A header shorter than five words has no room for its own fixed fields.
